analysis.one_liner: Makes research papers from federally funded science free online within a year of publication.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with support from a Republican and a Democrat, never left a Senate committee and died without a vote at the end of 2018.
analysis.plain_summary: Every federal agency that spends more than $100 million a year on outside research would have to create a policy requiring that the resulting peer-reviewed papers be posted in a free online government repository no later than 12 months after publication. Taxpayers who already paid for the research through taxes would be able to read the results without buying subscriptions or paying per-article fees charged by academic publishers. The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, patients, small researchers, students, and libraries. Anyone could read the results of research their tax dollars funded — for example, new medical findings — free, instead of paying $30 or more per article or relying on expensive university subscriptions [S3]. Scientists and innovators would also gain because the papers must be posted in formats that allow computer-based analysis and reuse [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires agencies spending over $100 million a year on extramural research to post the final peer-reviewed manuscripts of federally funded papers in a free online repository within 12 months of journal publication, preferably sooner [S3].

The bill's stated findings note that the federal government funds research expecting that shared discoveries will 'improve the lives and welfare of people of the United States,' and that the Internet makes this information available to 'every scientist, physician, educator, and citizen' [S3].
Papers must be provided in formats that enable productive reuse and computational analysis, not just locked PDFs, and agencies must make them easy to locate and preserve long-term [S3].
The GAO would report to Congress on how quickly papers actually reach the public repository and whether the policy effectively delivers free public access [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Academic journal publishers, whose business is selling subscriptions and per-article access to paywalls around publicly funded research. The bill allows a 12-month embargo (shorter is preferred) rather than immediate release, which softens but does not remove the cost to publishers. Federal agencies also bear the cost of maintaining repositories [S3].

drawbacks.text: Publishers argue that journals add real value — organizing peer review, editing, and dissemination — and that free public copies cut into subscription revenue that funds those services; the bill's 12-month embargo is an attempt to balance this, but publishers would still lose sales of the final version unless they consent to its replacement [S3].

Federal agencies would need to build and maintain digital repositories and review embargo-adjustment requests from publishers and other stakeholders, an administrative cost the bill does not fund separately [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is broad and the cost is concentrated: taxpayers have already paid for the research, and the bill simply requires they be able to read the results within a year, in reusable formats, while giving publishers a 12-month window to recoup subscription sales. The main honest trade-off is that agencies must pay for repositories and publishers lose some revenue; neither is close to the value of opening taxpayer-funded science to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, never receiving a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. John Cornyn introduced the bill on August 2, 2017, for himself and Sen. Ron Wyden, giving it a bipartisan Republican-Democratic sponsorship [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs on the day of introduction, its only action in the chamber [S5].
Two Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4], but the committee took no further action and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Academic journal publishers are better off because the bill died: their paywall subscriptions and per-article fees around federally funded research remain untouched, and taxpayers still pay to read work they funded.

for.name: Sen. John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require free public access to federally funded research papers.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Joined Cornyn in introducing the bill.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never reported it out; no hearing or markup appears in the record.

against.name: Academic journal publishers
against.what_they_did: Have publicly opposed similar open-access mandates in prior Congresses because free public copies undercut subscription and per-article revenue.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and a Democrat, with both cosponsors being Democrats; no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the full chamber is unknown.

industries.note: Publishers sell subscriptions and per-article access to research the public already paid for through taxes; free government repositories within 12 months would cut into that revenue. Their interest in keeping paywalls runs against readers, patients, and small institutions that cannot afford access.

industries.industry: Taxpayer-funded researchers and federal science agencies
industries.note: Researchers would gain wider readership and citations for their work but would take on repository-deposit duties; agencies would bear the cost of building and maintaining the repositories.
